title: Reading · Seq 1 Introduction to medical texts

options: Clinical trial results reported for the first time
questions.explanation: Primary literature reports original findings (new discoveries, trial results, case studies). Reviews and meta-analyses are secondary: they synthesize primary research.

questions.stem: Which statements about medical text sources are correct?
options: Historical treatises have no value for modern medicine
Peer-reviewed journals are considered more reliable than non-peer-reviewed publications
PubMed is provided by the National Library of Medicine
questions.explanation: Historical treatises (Edwin Smith Papyrus, Sushruta Samhita, Canon of Medicine) help understand the evolution of medical thought.

questions.stem: Match the text to its description:
options: The Canon of Medicine — medieval encyclopedia by Ibn Sina
Sushruta Samhita — modern textbook of surgery
Edwin Smith Papyrus — ancient treatise from Egypt
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine — the most widely read medical textbook
questions.explanation: Sushruta Samhita is an ancient treatise from India.

questions.stem: According to the course, the most efficient way to start reading a research article is to:
options: Read the abstract's conclusions to judge relevance
Read the whole paper from start to finish
questions.explanation: Experts recommend reviewing the abstract's conclusions first, then the methods and results, appraising at each step whether to continue.
The usual organization of an original research article, preceded by a structured abstract.

options: A meta-analysis is a primary research article
Systematic reviews address specific questions with defined methods for selecting papers
Narrative reviews give a qualitative overview of broad topics without a specific research question
A meta-analysis combines the statistical findings of several studies

questions.stem: About the title of a research article:
options: "Comparison of Microwave with Conventional Tissue Processing on Quality of Histological Sections" is a better title than "Microwave processing – A blessing for pathologists"
The best titles are descriptive and self-explanatory
It is the first point of attraction for readers
A vague, intriguing title is preferred
questions.explanation: A specific title tells the reader immediately what the study is about.

options: It is used to assess the statistical methods in detail
It helps readers quickly decide whether the paper is relevant
It is limited in word count
Most journals now require a structured abstract with subheadings
questions.explanation: Statistical methods are assessed in the Methods section.

questions.stem: Where are the aims of a study (and often the hypothesis) usually stated?
options: At the end of the introduction
questions.explanation: The introduction moves from background to literature to gap, and usually states the aims at its end; check later in the discussion whether the hypothesis was addressed.

questions.stem: Match each section with its role:
options: Introduction — statistical significance of the findings
Methods — study design, sample, data collection, statistics
Results — key findings, p-values, confidence intervals
questions.explanation: Statistical significance is reported in the Results.

questions.stem: In a case report, which section is described as "the heart of the report"?
questions.explanation: The case presentation gives background, history, findings and tests, interventions and follow-up in chronological order.

options: They require written informed consent from the patient or guardian
They are based on large population samples
questions.explanation: Case reports describe a single patient (rarely up to four).

questions.stem: Which features can make a clinical case worth publishing as a case report?
options: Educational merit, even for a common condition
questions.explanation: Also ethical or public-health relevance (ICMJE and leading journals).

questions.stem: Which tools are cited for critically appraising case reports?
questions.explanation: IMRAD is the structure of research articles; PubMed is a search database.

questions.stem: Research article (a) or case report (b)? Which matches are correct?
options: Aims at statistical significance and hypothesis testing — (b)
questions.explanation: Case reports aim at educational value and hypothesis generation, with selective references; hypothesis testing belongs to research articles.

questions.stem: "A 32-year-old woman presented with persistent cough and fever. Chest X-ray revealed consolidation in the right lower lobe..." This excerpt most likely comes from:
questions.explanation: A narrative about one patient's presentation and investigations is typical of a case report.

questions.stem: Which are reasons for reading journal articles listed in Table 1?
options: To stay updated in a field
questions.explanation: Eight reasons: stay updated, solve problems, understand disease, grasp fundamentals, generate research ideas, academic requirements, support own views, impress others. The course recommends learning basic biostatistics.
